question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what does the Navigation Rules require each operator to do?
choice_a: Neither vessel should alter course under any circumstance
choice_b: Each vessel should alter course to starboard (right) so they pass port-to-port, like cars on a two-lane road
choice_c: Both vessels should speed up to pass each other as quickly as possible
choice_d: Each vessel should turn to port (left) to pass starboard-to-starboard
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation between power-driven vessels, each is required to alter course to starboard so the vessels pass safely on each other's port side, mirroring the convention of driving on the right.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 14 - head-on situation)

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the "give-way" vessel required to take early and substantial action to avoid collision?
choice_a: Whichever vessel is larger, regardless of position
choice_b: Neither vessel needs to take any action
choice_c: The vessel that has the other vessel on its own starboard (right) side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel on its own port (left) side
explanation: In a crossing situation, the vessel that sees the other vessel on its own starboard side is the give-way vessel and must take early, substantial action -- typically altering course or slowing -- to avoid a close-quarters situation, while the other vessel is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 15 - crossing situation)

question: What must the "stand-on" vessel do in a crossing or overtaking situation?
choice_a: Immediately stop dead in the water regardless of surroundings
choice_b: Speed up as fast as possible to cross ahead of the other vessel
choice_c: Turn hard toward the give-way vessel
choice_d: Maintain its current course and speed so the give-way vessel can predict its position, unless collision becomes imminent, in which case it must take whatever action best avoids collision
explanation: The stand-on vessel is required to hold its course and speed to remain predictable to the give-way vessel, but if it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, the stand-on vessel must take whatever action will best avoid a collision, even though it is not at fault for needing to.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rules 15 and 17)

question: When one vessel is overtaking another on South Carolina waters, which vessel has the right-of-way?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken is the stand-on vessel and has the right-of-way; the overtaking vessel is the give-way vessel and must keep clear until well past and clear
choice_b: The overtaking (faster) vessel always has automatic right-of-way
choice_c: Whichever vessel honks first gets right-of-way
choice_d: Overtaking situations are not addressed by the Navigation Rules
explanation: The vessel being overtaken remains the stand-on vessel throughout the entire passing maneuver; the overtaking vessel is the give-way vessel and is obligated to keep well clear until it is finally past and clear of the vessel it passed.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 13 - overtaking)

question: Under the general right-of-way hierarchy used on South Carolina waters, which of the following vessels generally has the right-of-way over a typical recreational powerboat?
choice_a: There is no right-of-way hierarchy among different vessel types
choice_b: A vessel not under command or restricted in its ability to maneuver, such as a large commercial vessel confined to a narrow dredged channel
choice_c: A PWC always outranks every other vessel type
choice_d: A pontoon boat always outranks every commercial vessel
explanation: The general right-of-way hierarchy places vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, and vessels constrained by draft (such as large ships confined to a narrow dredged channel) above an ordinary recreational power-driven vessel, which must keep clear of them.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 18 - responsibilities between vessels)

question: What sound signal should a power-driven vessel give when it intends to alter its course to starboard while in sight of another vessel?
choice_b: Five or more short, rapid blasts
explanation: Under the maneuvering and warning signals of the Navigation Rules, one short blast (about one second) signals an intended course change to starboard; two short blasts signal a turn to port, and three short blasts signal operating astern propulsion.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 34 - maneuvering and warning signals)

question: What does five or more short, rapid blasts of a vessel's horn signal to nearby traffic?
choice_a: A greeting to other boaters passing by
choice_c: A signal that has no defined meaning under the Navigation Rules
choice_d: A danger or doubt signal, warning that the signaling vessel does not understand the other vessel's intentions or actions or believes a collision risk exists
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger/doubt signal, used when a vessel is unsure of another vessel's intent or actions, or believes the other vessel is not taking sufficient action to avoid collision.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 34 - danger/doubt signal)

question: How does the Navigation Rules generally treat right-of-way between a sailing vessel under sail alone and a power-driven vessel?
choice_a: The sailing vessel is generally the stand-on vessel and the power-driven vessel must generally keep clear, except when the sailing vessel is overtaking
choice_b: The power-driven vessel always has the right-of-way over a sailboat
choice_c: Right-of-way between sail and power vessels is decided purely by vessel size
choice_d: Sailing vessels have no right-of-way status under any rule
explanation: As a general rule, a sailing vessel under sail alone is the stand-on vessel relative to a power-driven vessel, and the power-driven vessel must keep out of the way -- except when the sailing vessel is overtaking, in which case the overtaking rule applies regardless of propulsion type.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 18)

question: In restricted or reduced visibility (such as fog, common on Lake Marion in the early morning), what sound signal must a power-driven vessel making way through the water sound?
choice_a: Three short blasts every ten minutes
choice_b: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than two minutes
choice_c: No sound signal is required in reduced visibility
choice_d: A continuous, unbroken horn blast for the entire duration of low visibility
explanation: A power-driven vessel underway and making way through the water in restricted visibility must sound one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than two minutes, alerting nearby vessels to its presence when it cannot be seen.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 35 - sound signals in restricted visibility)

question: Why must an operator navigating a narrow channel on South Carolina's Intracoastal Waterway keep as far to the starboard (right) edge as is safe and practicable?
choice_a: Vessels are required to travel down the exact center of every narrow channel
choice_b: Only sailing vessels are subject to narrow channel rules
choice_c: Because the Navigation Rules require vessels to hug the starboard edge of a narrow channel so opposing traffic can pass safely, similar to staying in your own lane on a road
choice_d: There is no rule governing narrow channel navigation
explanation: The narrow channel rule requires a vessel proceeding along a narrow channel to keep as near the outer limit of the channel on her starboard side as is safe and practicable, which is especially relevant on the Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway sections that pass through South Carolina.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 9 - narrow channels); relevance to South Carolina's Intracoastal Waterway

question: What is the boater's fundamental "lookout" obligation under the Navigation Rules at all times, day or night?
choice_a: A lookout is only required when another vessel is already within 50 feet
choice_b: Lookout duties may be delegated entirely to a passenger with no boating experience
choice_c: There is no lookout requirement in the Navigation Rules
choice_d: To maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing, using all available means appropriate to the circumstances, to fully assess the risk of collision
explanation: Rule 5 requires every vessel to maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing, as well as by all other available means, appropriate to the prevailing circumstances, so a full appraisal of the risk of collision can be made at all times.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rules, 33 CFR 83, Rule 5 - lookout)
